newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dollar opens sharply lower after Birch comment
newsitem.headline: NZ dollar opens sharply lower after Birch comment

text.p: * Finance Minister Birch says expects further fall late 1997
* Offshore market response seen as over-reaction
The New Zealand dollar opened sharply lower on Tuesday in reaction to Bill Birch's comments in Melbourne on Monday but dealers said overseas markets had over-reacted to the finance minister's view.
By 8.30 a.m. (2030 GMT) the currency was at US$0.6425/32 -- its lowest point since early March 1995 -- but was showing signs of stabilising after sinking to an overnight low of 0.6405.
Late on Monday the Kiwi had fallen to 0.6445/52, having started the session at 0.6520/27, around its lows of a week ago.
The Trade-Weighted Index was at 64.32 from 64.38 late on Monday.
Birch told Reuters in an interview in Melbourne that he expected the Kiwi to fall further towards the end of 1997.

"I expect we will see it come down," Birch said in response to a question. "They (the Reserve Bank) are foreshadowing further easings towards the end of this year, so you are likely to get a little more easing," he said.
But dealers said the market may have got a little ahead of itself, especially given the sharp decline of recent weeks.
The New Zealand dollar traded on Friday at 0.6570 -- having lost four U.S. cents since early June.
"Birch is talking further out at the moment. I would be surprised if the RBNZ is really sanctioning the speed of this move," the dealer said.
Dealers expect the pattern of the last few days -- offshore selling and slight retracements locally -- to remain in place for the time being.
Dealers noted that debt yields had risen sharply in response to currency weakness.
"That may catch some hot money, given that yields are good and that we have already lost quite a percentage off the currency," said one dealer.
There was a perception that the currency would not fall much further while yields continued to ratchet up.
